analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers and businesses elect a 17-19% flat tax instead of the income tax, and repeals the estate and gift taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, drew 8 Republican cosponsors and no further action, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an optional flat tax: anyone who elected it would pay 19% for two years and 17% after, on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits, minus a large standard deduction, in place of the regular income tax and the alternative minimum tax. Businesses could elect a 17-19% tax on gross active income minus their costs and wages. Separately and unconditionally, the bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for everyone. It also requires a two-thirds vote of either chamber to raise the flat tax rate or shrink the deductions later.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and the wealthy gain the most. The flat tax would tax only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation - dividends, interest, and capital gains would not be taxed - so people whose income comes largely from investments would owe little or nothing under it. Wealthy estates gain regardless of whether anyone elects the flat tax, because the estate and gift taxes are repealed outright for all deaths and gifts after 2007. Businesses gain a 17% tax on income after deducting costs and wages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and wealthy estates

how_it_helps.text: Any individual or business could make an irrevocable election to pay a flat tax of 19% for the first two years and 17% thereafter, in place of regular income tax rates and the alternative minimum tax.

Individual taxable income would be wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation minus a standard deduction of $12,790 for singles, $16,330 for heads of household, or $25,580 for joint filers, plus $5,510 per dependent, with inflation adjustments after 2008.
Business taxable income would be gross active income reduced by the cost of business inputs, cash wages, and retirement contributions, taxed at the same 19%-then-17% rates.
The estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would be repealed for all decedents dying and transfers made after December 31, 2007, with no election required.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays first: the bill repeals a major tax on the largest estates and offers a deep rate cut to anyone who elects the flat tax, and the lost revenue would have to be made up through borrowing or other taxes. State and local governments and nonprofit employers would pay a new 17-19% tax on the value of noncash benefits, such as health insurance, provided to their employees. Electing families would give up all tax credits, including the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury, then all future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Electors would be allowed no tax credits of any kind, so low- and moderate-income families who rely on the earned income tax credit or child tax credit would come out behind under the flat tax and could not switch back after electing.
The estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would be repealed outright for everyone, a tax cut concentrated on the largest estates, with no replacement revenue specified in the bill.

Employers that are tax-exempt organizations or federal, state, or local government agencies would owe a new 17-19% tax on the value of noncash employee benefits, raising the cost of public-sector and nonprofit compensation.

Any future bill to raise the flat tax rate or reduce the standard deduction or business deductions could not pass either chamber without a two-thirds vote, locking in the lower rates against ordinary majority rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For high earners and wealthy families the arithmetic is clearly favorable: investment income goes untaxed and large estates go untaxed. For a middle-income wage earner the flat tax could be roughly comparable to current taxes once the large standard deductions are counted, but electing means losing every tax credit, and the choice is irrevocable. The bill never addresses the revenue it removes, so the cost would land on everyone else through debt or other taxes. The voluntary design limits the immediate damage to families who would lose under it, but the mandatory estate tax repeal applies whether or not anyone elects.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees on the day it was introduced, the committees never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on February 14, 2007, and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Rules.
Eight Republican House members cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
After the sponsor's introductory remarks in March 2007, no committee action, floor action, or vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal Treasury are better off because the bill died: the estate tax on the largest estates stayed on the books for the life of the Congress, and no revenue was shifted away from investment income. The bill's intended beneficiaries - high earners, wealthy estates, and businesses seeking the 17% rate - are worse off than they would have been had it passed.

for.name: Rep. Michael Burgess
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 14, 2007 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in March 2007.

for.name: 8 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the flat tax and estate tax repeal bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral - no markup, no vote, no report - leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters - the sponsor and eight cosponsors - were Republicans, and the bill never advanced in a House controlled by Democrats.

industries.note: The estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would be repealed outright, with no election required, eliminating the tax that falls only on the largest estates. The lost revenue would otherwise fund the government or reduce taxes elsewhere.

The flat tax counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits as taxable income; dividends, interest, and capital gains are not included. Investors who elect would pay tax only on their wages while their investment income goes untaxed.

Businesses could elect a 17% tax (19% for two years) on gross active income minus costs, wages, and retirement contributions, in place of the corporate income tax and the alternative minimum tax. The revenue loss is borne by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: State and local governments and tax-exempt employers
industries.note: Employers that are governments or tax-exempt organizations would owe a new 17-19% tax on the value of noncash benefits, such as health insurance, provided to their employees, raising the cost of public and nonprofit payrolls.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Electing taxpayers would file a simple return based on wages minus a standard deduction, reducing the market for filing help - though only for those who elect, so the effect is limited.
